results.title: Chapter 26 Quasi-Experimental Methods | A Guide on Data Analysis
results.content: Because quasi-experiments rely on observational or naturally occurring data, the assumptions required to identify causal effects are generally more stringent, less testable, and more vulnerable to violation than in randomized settings. If \(\mathcal{N}(i) \neq \emptyset\), then SUTVA is violated, necessitating alternative modeling approaches such as **spatial econometrics**, **network-based causal inference**, or **graph-based treatment effect estimation**. Unlike structural models, which rely on extensive theoretical assumptions, design-based methods leverage **exogenous events, policy changes, or assignment rules** to infer causal effects with **minimal modeling assumptions**. The model-based perspective in causal inference relies on statistical modeling techniques to estimate treatment effects, rather than exploiting exogenous sources of variation as in design-based approaches. Unlike other quasi-experimental designs that leverage external assignment mechanisms (e.g., a cutoff, policy change, or natural experiment), model-based methods assume that confounding can be adequately adjusted for using statistical techniques alone. Model-based methods allow researchers to estimate treatment effects even when exogenous variation is unavailable. Regression models estimate causal effects by controlling for observed confounders.
